Helbon
HEL-bon
proper noun
Hebrew Chelbon, “fruitful” or “fat,” a place near Damascus famed for its wine, named in the lament over Tyre.

Biblical Definition

Helbon appears once, as a luxury on the manifest of a doomed merchant-city. In Ezekiel’s great lamentation over Tyre, the prophet catalogues the riches that flowed into her markets: “Damascus was thy merchant in the multitude of the wares of thy making, for the multitude of all riches; in the wine of Helbon, and white wool” (Eze 27:18). The wine of Helbon was a byword for the finest vintage, poured, ancient records say, at the tables of kings. It came to Tyre, that queen of commerce for whom the prophet was bidden, “take up a lamentation for Tyrus” (Eze 27:2). Tyre had enriched the earth: “thou didst enrich the kings of the earth with the multitude of thy riches and of thy merchandise” (Eze 27:33). Yet all her wealth, the wine of Helbon and the white wool and the treasures of the seas, could not save her from the judgment of God. Helbon thus stands as a small emblem of luxury under sentence. The wine is good in itself, a gift of God to gladden the heart of man; but the heart that makes riches and pleasure its trust is warned: “Look not thou upon the wine when it is red” (Pro 23:31). The finest vintage cannot ransom a soul, and the proudest market falls when its cup of iniquity is full.

Webster 1828 Definition

A place near Damascus famed for its wine, named in the lament over Tyre (Eze 27:18); an emblem of the luxury that cannot ransom a city under the judgment of God.

HELBON, a place near Damascus renowned for its fine wine.

Its name means “fruitful” or “fat.”

Named once, in the lamentation over Tyre (Eze 27:18).

Its wine was a byword for the vintage of kings.

An emblem of luxury under the sentence of God upon Tyre.

Key Scripture

Eze 27:18 — "Damascus was thy merchant in the multitude of the wares of thy making, for the multitude of all riches; in the wine of Helbon, and white wool."

Eze 27:2 — "Now, thou son of man, take up a lamentation for Tyrus;"

Eze 27:33 — "thou didst enrich the kings of the earth with the multitude of thy riches and of thy merchandise."

Pro 23:31 — "Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup"

Modern Corruption

The place of the wine of kings, named in Tyre’s lament; the entry recovers that no luxury can ransom a soul or a city from the judgment of God.

expand to see more

Helbon’s single mention names a luxury — the finest wine — flowing into the market of doomed Tyre. The wine itself is a good gift of God, given to gladden the heart of man; the corruption is not in the vintage but in the trust. Tyre made her riches her god and reckoned herself untouchable.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that abundance is a stewardship, not a security. The consumer age, like Tyre, heaps to itself the wine of Helbon and the wares of the world and imagines that comfort is salvation. But the finest cup cannot ransom a soul, and the wealthiest city falls when its iniquity is full. Let the Christian receive God’s good gifts with thanksgiving and sobriety, remembering that the treasure which endures is laid up in heaven, not poured in the goblets of Tyre.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Chelbon, “fruitful,” a place near Damascus famed for the wine named in Tyre’s lament.

Helbon — Hebrew Chelbon, “fruitful” or “fat.”

A place near Damascus, renowned for fine wine.

Named once, among the wares of Tyre (Eze 27:18).

Its wine was proverbial for the tables of kings.

An emblem of luxury that cannot save from judgment.

Usage

"The wine of Helbon came to the markets of Tyre."

"Damascus traded Helbon’s wine and white wool for Tyre’s wares."

"Helbon preaches that no luxury can ransom a soul from God’s judgment."
